prologue.title: Now
prologue.subtitle: A machine shed, two hours of gravel from town

norway.title: Norway
norway.subtitle: A fjord in the west, about the year 870

knows_he_bled.description: Aud said the uncle left bleeding, and that somebody in the hall did it

hrapp_owes.description: You kept the smith alive in front of the hall

walter.name: Walter
walter.notes: Your uncle. The hall calls him Unkel, having taken the word for his name.

kol.name: Kol
kol.notes: A boy of about eleven, with a dog. He finds everything first and tells everyone.

thorgrim.name: Thorgrim Ketilsson
thorgrim.notes: The hersir. It is his hall, and his half pound of silver.

aud.name: Aud Ketilsdóttir
aud.notes: Thorgrim's sister. The keys are hers.

hrapp.name: Hrapp
hrapp.notes: The smith. He does your uncle's voice.

hild.name: Hild
hild.notes: Gyda's apprentice at the healing. She keeps a stick.

finn.name: Finn Ormsson
finn.notes: Orm's son. He builds by looking.

eyvind.name: Eyvind
eyvind.notes: A skald. He goes between the halls and says who is dead. Invented; not the Eyvind of the next century.

ulfar.name: Ulfar
ulfar.notes: Hrapp's brother, one farm up the water. His boy died at harvest.

welder.label: A welder
welder.description: You join steel for a living and have the forearms to prove it. You have never done it without electricity.

nurse.label: A nurse
nurse.description: Eleven years on a surgical ward, most of them nights. You know what a wound ought to look like on the third day.

teacher.label: A history teacher
teacher.description: You have explained the fall of Rome to fifteen-year-olds every spring for nine years. Nobody has asked you to prove any of it until now.

engineer.label: An engineer
engineer.description: You can say why a bridge stands up and what it will cost. Other people have always done the building.

rider.label: Rode as a child
rider.description: Every Saturday until you were sixteen. Somebody else always caught the horse, and somebody else fed it.

charm.label: Easy to like
charm.description: People tell you things. You have never been sure what you do to cause it, and have learned not to ask.

martial.label: Martial arts
martial.description: A brown belt, earned twice a week in a hall that smelled of feet. Nobody there was trying to kill you.

fencer.label: Fenced
fencer.description: Three years of foil, with a mask, a referee and a rule about whose turn it was.

speaker.label: Used to a room
speaker.description: You can stand up in front of two hundred people and be heard at the back. What you said when you got there has varied.

hunter.label: Hunts
hunter.description: A week every autumn, with a rifle and a flask, and the truck forty yards behind you.

sailor.label: Sails
sailor.description: Summers on a lake, in a boat that belonged to somebody's father. You know where the wind is before you know you have looked.

farm.label: Raised on a farm
farm.description: Chores before school for sixteen years. Animals have never frightened you, and have never impressed you either.

tall.label: Tall
tall.description: You have found most door frames the same way.

slight.label: Slight
slight.description: People hand you things to hold.

broad.label: Broad
broad.description: Strangers ask you to help them move house.

blunt.label: Blunt
blunt.description: You say it, and afterwards you find out whether you should have.

quiet.label: Quiet
quiet.description: You are often taken to be agreeing.

cheerful.label: Cheerful
cheerful.description: It has been held against you.

the_door.label: Through the stone
the_door.description: This is as far as the prototype goes: the whole of the Norway visit. Japan is next, and is not built yet. Nor are the four years.

n_hill.title: The hill
n_hill.text:
You are up to the shins in heather and the rain is coming in from the side.

The frame has not come with you, nor the shed. Behind you is a boulder about the size of a grain truck, with a streak of white quartz down the face of it, and you take a good look at that streak, since it is the only way home you know about.

Somebody has been at the quartz with a nail. Cut into it, at about the height of a short man's shoulder, are a letter and a row of marks.

::clue boulder_tally::

You count them twice. You had thought he had only done this the once.

Then you turn around, and it is some time before you do anything else.

The hill falls away below your boots in grey rock and rusty bracken, down to water that lies a long way under you, black-green and so still that it holds the mountains upside down. It runs inland between walls of rock that go up into the cloud and do not come out again. Across from you a waterfall hangs on the far wall, a white thread of it, too far off to hear.

There is no wire anywhere in the sky and no road cut into the other shore, and it is quieter than you knew a place could be. You would have liked somebody to be standing next to you, to say so to.
[break]
On a shelf of green by the water stands a building, longer than your uncle's shed and much lower, bowed along its length like the hull of a boat turned over. Grass is growing on the roof. Smoke leaks out along the ridge, having found no chimney, and lies down flat in the rain. Smaller roofs stand about it, and strips of field gone pale with stubble, and on the shingle below are two boats drawn up side by side. Even from this height you know the line of them, the long rise to the stem that somebody drew in one stroke.[if trait.sailor]

The wind is coming up the water from the sea, and the smoke agrees with you. Both boats have been hauled out with their sterns to it, by somebody who did not have to look either.[/if]

The only other one you have seen was in a museum, black and cracked, propped on steel behind glass. These two are the colour of dark honey and they are wet. Whoever built them is very likely down there under the grass roof, keeping dry, and could build you a third if you had anything to pay him with.

You try your phone. It has sixty-one per cent and nobody to call, and you put it away.

By now you are cold enough to notice. You get into the lee of the boulder and collect sticks, with some confidence, having lit fires before, in a pit, on a dry evening, with a firelighter. Wet heather held over the lighter gives off steam. The bark of a small bent birch does no more. You take out the note and consider it, and decide your uncle would want it kept. By the time the lighter is too hot to hold you have produced a smell.
[break]
"Hvat ertu?"

A boy is standing a few yards up the hill with a dog and a stick. He might be eleven. His wool is the colour of the hillside, which accounts for how near he has got, and the dog beside him has plainly reached a decision about you and is waiting for him to catch up.

The brass thing clicks twice behind your ear, like a relay closing.

"What are you?" he says again. This time it reaches you in English, half a beat after his mouth has finished. He has asked what, you notice, and not who.

[if manner == blunt]"Cold," you tell him.[elif manner == quiet]You hold up your hands, which have gone the colour of the boulder, and let him work it out.[elif manner == cheerful]"Cold, thanks," you tell him, as you might to somebody at a bus stop.[else]"Lighting a fire," you tell him, over the place where there is no fire.[/if]

[if manner == quiet]He frowns at you as people do at the hard of hearing.[else]Your throat does something to the words on their way out that you had no part in, and he frowns as people do at a heavy accent.[/if] Then he looks at your sticks, and at the lighter, which you are slow to cover.

He crouches down. Out of the pouch on his belt come a curl of steel, a flake of stone and a pinch of black felted stuff, and with his back to the wind and a knee on your sticks he has a flame going before you have the lighter back in your pocket. He feeds it with bark he has been carrying inside his shirt, where it keeps dry. His hands manage all this alone, because the rest of him is studying your jacket.
[break]
"Can I?" he says, and has hold of the zip before you answer. He runs it down and up and watches the teeth shut behind the tab, and does it again, eleven times in all. You keep count, there being nothing else for you to do at your own fire.

"Unkel had one of these," he says. "On his trousers."

"You know my uncle?"

"Everyone knows Unkel. He owes Thorgrim a ship."

After that he gets round to what you are carrying.

[if kit == bag]He has it open before you can decide whether to stop him.

[if occupation == welder]The helmet he puts on, and takes off again directly, having found that it makes the world dark. The gloves he approves of. Then he comes to the file. He tries its edge with his thumb and draws it once along the back of his fire-steel, where it lifts a bright curl and leaves a flat, and he looks at the flat for some time.

"You are a smith," he says. "Hrapp is our smith." He puts the file back with more care than he took it out. "Hrapp is going to hate you."[elif occupation == nurse]The scissors he approves of. The gloves he blows up, ties off and gives to the dog, which does not want one. Then he finds the stethoscope, and after some thought puts the wrong end in his mouth. You fit it to his ears and hold the other end against his chest. He listens to himself for a while, and afterwards to the dog, and you can see him deciding which of them is the better made.

"You are a healer," he says. "Gyda is our healer." He hands the thing back by its tubing, as he would a live eel. "Gyda is going to hate you."[elif occupation == teacher]It holds thirty-one essays on the causes of the First World War, which you had meant to mark at your uncle's kitchen table. He turns over a good many pages before he sees that the marks on them are all different, and that somebody made every one. The red pen he clicks until you take it from him. He draws a line with it across the back of his hand and holds the hand out to the rain to see whether it will stay.

"You make marks for remembering," he says. "Ulf remembers for us, and he needs no marks." He gives you back the essays, in no order. "Ulf is going to hate you."[else]The hard hat he puts on and keeps on. The calculator he shakes, in case there is something in it. Then he finds the tape, draws out an arm's length of it, and lets go. When it has finished coming back at him he does it again, and then he measures the dog, which is forty-one inches from nose to tail and holds still for it.

"You measure things," he says. "Orm builds our ships and he measures nothing. He looks." He winds the tape in by hand, slowly, to see where it goes. "Orm is going to hate you."[/if]

He appears to be looking forward to it. He says he is called Kol, and he carries the bag down the hill himself, shouting before the yard is in earshot that he has found something on the mountain and that it was he who found it.[elif kit == notebook]It is open on your knee, where you had been hunting for a page about fire. This is the page you have instead.

::clue notebook_people::

"You're Kol," you say.

The boy stops with his hand on the dog's neck. "Who gave you my name?"

You have no answer he would like, so you hold up the book. He looks at the marks on the page as he might at the tracks of an animal he had only been told about, and he does not come any nearer to them. Your uncle has gone round the last line a good many times, you notice, and not all with the same pen.

Kol goes down the hill well ahead of you and does not wait at the turns. When you reach the yard on your own, a good while after him, a number of people have found work to do near the door, and it is clear that the news has arrived and that it was about the names.[else]He looks into it and is not much struck. You tear a corner off the sugar and shake some into his palm, and he takes it for salt and licks it up out of manners.

He stands quite still. Then he cleans the palm thoroughly, looks into the sack to see how much more of it there is, and ties the neck himself, with a knot you would not like to have to undo.

"Do not give that to anybody on the way down," he says. "They will only want it."

He lets you know that he is called Kol and that you may walk behind him. In the yard he informs a woman carrying buckets, and after her the hens, that the stranger is his, that he found it, and that nobody is to touch the sack.[/if]

choices.text: Go down to the hall.

n_hall.title: Unkel's water
n_hall.text:
Your boots were made for a flat floor, and you go down most of the hill sitting.[if trait.rider]

There is a horse in the yard, about the size of a large pony and the colour of the hill. It looks you over as the ones at the riding school used to, and you can tell that it has come to the same view.[/if]

The door of the long building is cut for people who know where the lintel is.[if looks == tall] You find out where it is.[elif looks == broad] You go through it at an angle, as a sofa would.[elif looks == slight] You pass under it with room to spare, and it is the last thing you do all day as well as the people who live here.[/if]

Inside it is dark and far bigger than it looked from the hill. A fire burns in a trench down the middle of the floor, a truck-length of it, and its light climbs the posts and gives up before it reaches the roof. The posts are whole trees. Somebody has carved every one of them, from the floor to as high as you can see, with beasts that bite each other and are knotted so tight you could not get a nail in between. It is the best thing you have ever seen made by hand, and nobody in the room is looking at it. The place smells of smoke and wet dog, of meat and of a good many people, [if looks == forgettable]none of whom has turned round. You stand inside the door for long enough to learn the price of a ewe. In the end it is a small child who points.[else]some thirty of whom have turned to look at you. The talk stops one bench at a time, working up from the door to the far end, until the fire is the loudest thing in the room.[/if]
[break]
Near the hearth sits a man with his sleeve pushed up and a cut across the heel of his hand. An old woman has him by the wrist, and a girl is lifting a pot off the fire between two sticks.

"Eighteen," the girl is saying. "Nineteen. Twenty. That is four."

"That is three," says the man with the hand.

"It is four, Bjorn. I have my thumb on it."

"Then your thumb moved."

They count it again to settle the matter. Only when the girl has reached twenty does the old woman pour, and the man lets his breath out through his teeth, and she ties up the hand in a cloth out of the same pot.

"Unkel's water," Kol says, in the tone of a boy with a slow pupil. "You boil it for a hundred. Nobody is going to count a hundred for a pot, so we count twenty, five times." He lifts his chin at the man. "Bjorn put an axe in his own leg last winter and it should have come off. Unkel washed it in his water every day and shouted at anybody who touched it, and Bjorn still has the leg."

"Did he say why it works?"

"He said there are beasts in water, too small to see, and the boiling kills them." Kol considers you, to find out whether you are the kind of person who would believe that. "Nobody listened to that part. But the leg stayed on. So we boil it, and we leave out the beasts."
[break]
At the head of the fire, in the only seat with a back, a man of about fifty has watched your arrival without moving anything but his eyes. He is built along the same lines as the posts. He lifts one finger, and you go up the hall.

[if kit == bag]"Kol tells me he has found something useful," Thorgrim says. "The last one off that hill told me he was useful as well."[elif kit == notebook]"Kol tells me you had his name before he gave it," Thorgrim says. "Have you mine?" You have, and you say it, and the people on the bench nearest you discover that there is room further along.[else]You put the pepper and a card of needles on the board in front of him. He opens the tin and sneezes, and is pleased with it. "Unkel came with his hands empty and went away with them full," Thorgrim says. "You have it the other way about."[/if]

"You are his kin, though. You have his clothes, and you stand in my hall as he did, as if somebody were about to explain it to you." There is some laughing at this. "He ate at my fire from hay-time until the leaves turned, and he ate well. He kept Bjorn's leg on, and reminded us of it most evenings. I liked him. He said he could build me a ship that would sail into the wind. I asked how, and he drew it in the ashes, and it was a handsome drawing. I gave him half a pound of silver to buy iron. Six nights ago he went up that hill with it and has not come down."

"What do you want with a ship that sails into the wind?"

"There is a king working his way along this coast," Thorgrim says, "and he has the wind behind him. Tonight you are my guest. Tomorrow you are Unkel's kin, and you have what Unkel owes. We will talk about my ship when you have eaten."
[break]
[if hero.sex == male]You are given the end of the bench nearest the door, among the dogs, where a stranger sits until the hall has made up its mind.[else]You are given the end of the cross-bench at the far wall, where the women of the house sit, and where you are gone over a good deal more thoroughly than Thorgrim troubled to.[/if]

A girl brings you a basin of water and a cloth and holds them out. You look at the basin and then at the girl. It has been a long day, and you cannot honestly say whether the water is for drinking. You settle it by wiping your hands down your jeans, to show you mean well.

A woman has stopped behind the girl to watch this. She is about your age, in a dress of the dark red that a gate goes when it has rusted properly, with the sleeves shoved back from work she has not finished, and at her belt hangs a ring of keys, a dozen or more. People along the benches drew in their feet as she came. Her face, through the whole business with the basin, stays exactly where it was, and you suspect that took some doing.

"Hands in the water," she says. "After that the cloth, and after that you eat. Unkel had it by his second month."

A bowl arrives with something grey and hot in it, and barley in that. No spoon arrives. Along both benches people are taking spoons out of belts and sleeves, having brought their own, as people evidently do. She unhooks one of pale horn from beside the keys, worn thin along one edge, and holds it out, and keeps hold of her end when you take yours.

"I have had this longer than I had my husband," she says. "I want it back."

Kol informs you, at no great pains to be quiet, that this is Aud, Thorgrim's sister, and that the keys are hers and so is whatever they open.

choices.text: Eat.

n_choke.title: The smith's throat
n_choke.text:
Across the fire a man with burned forearms has been telling his end of the bench about Unkel, and doing the voice. He does it well. You know it for your uncle at once, through a brass ear and eleven hundred years, and you find that you have missed the sound of him. Halfway through a sentence about the ship he stops.

Nobody minds at first. He has a mouthful, and a man with a mouthful is allowed to stop. Then he gets to his feet, and puts a hand flat on the board, and the other to his throat, and makes no sound at all. The man next to him laughs and thumps him between the shoulders. The smith's face has gone the colour of a plum.

[if occupation == nurse]You have done this eleven times, twice on the same patient, and you are over the bench and round the fire before you have decided to be.[else]You once spent a wet afternoon in a church hall being shown this on a rubber torso by a man called Keith. You find, to your surprise, that it took.[/if]

You get behind him, put your arms round his middle, make a fist under his ribs with the other hand over it, and pull.
[break]
It is only now, with your arms round a stranger from behind in a hall full of his kin, that you see how it looks. Three men are on their feet. One of them has a knife out, the short one he was eating with, and is coming round the end of the bench with it. You pull again, and something leaves the smith at speed and lands in the fire, where it hisses.

He breathes in, with a noise like a door being forced. Then he calls you something the brass ear declines to translate.

Nobody in the hall is talking. The man with the knife has stopped, though he has not put it away.

"What," says Thorgrim, "did you do to my smith?"

choices.text: Tell him it is a hold your people use for a bone in the throat.
Tell him the man was choking and now he is not, and sit down.
Tell him how it works.

n_hold.title: A hold
n_hold.text:
"It is a hold," you say. "Where I come from it is taught for a bone in the throat. The fist goes here, under the ribs, and you pull up and in."

Thorgrim nods slowly. A hold is a thing a hall understands. They wrestle here all winter, having little else to do, and the man with the knife puts it away and asks to be shown where the fist goes.

You show it on Kol, who has volunteered by standing closest. Before the bowls are empty there are three pairs of boys by the door doing it to one another, and one of them has been sick. The old woman who poured the water comes down the hall to ask whether there is a word that is said with it. You tell her there is not. She is disappointed in you, and you gather from Kol that there will be a word by tomorrow whether you supply one or not.
[break]
Aud sits down on the bench beside you, which makes the bench go quiet.

"'Where I come from it is taught,'" she says. "That was well put. Unkel would have told us why it works, and Hrapp would have died of listening."

"It is taught, where I come from."

"I do not doubt it." She takes back her spoon, looks it over, and hangs it by the keys. "Hrapp will not thank you. He hates to owe, and he liked Unkel less than anybody here did. I would stay out of the forge for a day or two."

choices.text: Find somewhere to sleep.

n_silent.title: Your barley
n_silent.text:
"He was choking," you say. "Now he isn't."

You step back over the bench, sit down and pick up your bowl, which is still warm.

For a little while nothing happens. After that the hall does your explaining for you, at some length, and you eat through it. By the time you reach the bottom of the barley you have been a wrestler from the east, and you have been one of Unkel's people, who are known to have healing in their hands. The old woman who poured the water holds that you squeezed a thing out of Hrapp that had been in him since midwinter, and that he is better without it. Nobody asks you which. Thorgrim has you moved four places up the bench, into the warm, and somebody you have not met fills your cup.
[break]
Aud comes for her spoon when you have finished with it.

"You let them tell it," she says. "Unkel never once managed that. He would have been on his feet by now, drawing in the ashes."

"There wasn't much to tell."

"No." She turns your hand over, looks at the palm as if it might say more than you had, and gives it back. "I will want to hear it, all the same. It need not be tonight."

choices.text: Find somewhere to sleep.

n_explain.title: Two pipes
n_explain.text:
"There are two pipes in the throat," you say. "One is for air and the other is for food. The meat went down the one for air. There was still air in his chest, under the meat, so I squeezed the chest, and the air pushed it out."

Bjorn feels his own neck with his good hand. The old woman who poured the water asks, quite reasonably, why in that case a man cannot breathe and swallow together all day long. You tell her there is a flap that closes.

"A door," says someone further down. "In the throat."

"A small one."

You hear it, then, as they are hearing it. Thorgrim looks at you for a time without unkindness.

"Unkel talked like this," he says. "The beasts in the water."
[break]
Hrapp, who owes you his life, has moved a place further down the bench from you. Several people have found something to look at in their bowls. Aud takes you by the sleeve, walks you the length of the hall to the door post, and stands with her back to the room.

"Was it true? About the pipes."

"Yes."

"I thought it might be. Unkel's were mostly true as well." She keeps her voice under the noise, which is starting up again behind her. "They will have a true thing out of your hands any day of the year. Out of your mouth it is only talk. The last one here who talked like that went up the hill six nights ago with his hand wrapped in his shirt."

"Whose knife was it?"

"Eat your barley," Aud says. "And I will have my spoon back when you have."

choices.text: Find somewhere to sleep.

n_night.title: The first night
n_night.text:
The fire is banked for the night, and the hall goes to sleep around you all at once, as a barn does. Rain is falling on the grass over your head. It is a roof you would very much like to tell your mother about, and you have been asked not to.

[if kit == bag]Your bag is under your head, and you have a hand through the strap.[elif kit == notebook]The notebook is inside your jacket, where nobody can ask to see it.[else]Kol has the sack, and is asleep on top of it.[/if] [if road.first == hold]By the door, two boys are still practising the hold on each other in the dark.[elif road.first == silent]Further down the bench somebody is still explaining you to somebody else, and getting it wrong.[else]Nobody has lain down within an arm's length of you.[/if]

Tomorrow you are Unkel's kin.

choices.text: Sleep.

n_morning.title: Unkel's kin
n_morning.text:
You are woken by a dog, which has decided in the night that you are furniture.

The hall in the morning is grey light through the smoke and people stepping over one another. Nobody has forgotten last night. [if road.first == hold]By the fire two small boys have a third in the hold, and the old woman who poured the water is overseeing it. She has a word for it now. The word is Unkelstak, Unkel's grip, which is hard on your uncle, who never did it, and harder on you.[elif road.first == silent]You gather, from talk that nobody troubles to lower, that the stories about you were settled into one overnight. You are a healer who wrestles. You could have done worse.[else]The bench has room on either side of you this morning, as it had last night. A small girl comes over to look at your throat, and is called away.[/if]

Aud puts a bowl into your hands on her way past, without stopping. "Thorgrim is at the shore," she says. "He would like you to see what your kinsman left him. Eat first. You will want it in you."

Kol is waiting at the door with the dog. He has been up the hill already, since he goes up the hill every morning, and he reports that the wet smell by the white stone is fainter than it was yesterday. He says it as he might tell you a ewe was lame. You find that you do not like it.

choices.text: Go down to the shore.

n_keel.title: The ship that is not there
n_keel.text:
The boat shed is open at both ends, like your uncle's, and smells of tar and new wood.[if hero.sex == female] Half of it is given over to a sail, a great brown weight of wool laid across three trestles, with four women sewing at it. They look up together, like one animal with eight eyes. There is an empty stool at the fourth trestle.[/if]

[if hero.sex == female]In the other half lies your uncle's ship.[else]In the middle of it lies your uncle's ship.[/if] It is a keel, a stem, a stern and four planks up each side, and there it stops. Grass has not had time to grow through it, but something has made a nest in the bow.

"Orm laid it at midsummer," Thorgrim says. "Your kinsman stood where you are standing and told him where everything went. Orm has built ships since before I had a beard. He did as he was told as far as the fourth plank. Then he put down his axe, and said he would not put another on a thing he could not see in his head." He nods at a big grey man at the far end of the shed, who is fitting a rib and does not look round. "I have paid for the oak."

On a flat stone by the keel is a wooden bowl, upside down. Thorgrim lifts it off as you would lift a lid to show a guest the dinner.

::clue ash_drawing::

"Nobody has been allowed to sweep there," he says.
[break]
[if occupation == engineer]You know it at once, because you drew it yourself, at about ten, on the back of an exercise book. It is a dinghy. He has given a ship of this size the sail off a holiday boat, and nothing under the water to stop it going sideways. It would sail into the wind for as long as it took to fall over.[elif occupation == welder]You cannot say whether it would sail. You can say that the mast in the drawing is held up by four fittings that would each need a lathe to make, and that he has drawn them with some love. He always did like a fitting.[elif occupation == nurse]You could not tell a good ship from a bathtub. You do know the hand. He has drawn the wind as an arrow, and you are quite sure that if the ash had been finer he would have labelled it.[else]You have seen that sail in books, on boats from seas a long way south of here. Nobody on this coast has seen it, and from what you remember nobody on this coast will take it up for a very long time. He has not so much promised Thorgrim a ship as a different history.[/if]

"Three days," Thorgrim says. "Orm says the weather holds three days, and after that nothing is built until spring. You are his kin. Go where you can be of use, and at the noon meal tell me what kind of use it was."

He goes. You are left with the keel, and the rest of his farm.

choices.text: Stay in the boat shed.
Go to where they boil the cloths.
Go to the forge.

n_boat.title: The fifth plank
n_boat.text:
There is a young man under the keel with an adze, taking off shavings as long as your arm. He comes out when the light changes, looks at you, and then looks at your hands, which is evidently what people here do first.

"Finn," he says. "Orm's son. You are the other one."

"The other one."

"Unkel's. He stood there for a month and told my father how a ship is built." He says it without heat. "My father has not been the same since. I thought it was the best month we ever had."

He builds, you find, by looking. There is no drawing in the shed and no measure.[if occupation == engineer] You put the tape back in your pocket.[/if] He holds a plank against the last one, looks along it with one eye shut, takes it away, and removes a sliver you would not have known was there. Then it fits along its whole length, to the thickness of a hair. He has cut a mark in the door post for every plank that went on the first time.

::clue finn_tally::
[break]
"You may hold that end," he says.[if hero.sex == female] The women at the sail stop sewing, to see whether you will.[/if]

You hold that end. It is the fifth plank, the one his father would not put on, and Finn is putting it on because nobody has told him not to. It is green oak, split and not sawn, and it has to take a twist toward the stem. Halfway round the twist it speaks. A crack starts at the edge by the third rivet hole and opens toward the middle of the plank, a finger's length, and stops there to think about it.

Finn says a word the brass ear lets through untouched.

[if occupation == welder]You know cracks. A crack runs because its end is sharp, and you stop it by making the end round: you drill a hole just ahead of it, and it has nowhere left to go. You have done it on a stock trailer and on a fuel tank, and once on your own truck.[elif occupation == engineer]You know cracks. A crack runs because its end is sharp, and you stop it by making the end round: a hole drilled just ahead of it, and it has nowhere left to go. You once wrote four pages recommending this for a footbridge, and a man with a drill did it in a morning.[else]You once watched a man in a garage do this to a crack in a windscreen. He drilled a small hole just ahead of the end of it, and the crack ran into the hole and stopped, having nowhere sharp left to go. It cost forty dollars, and you thought at the time that it was a trick.[/if]

choices.text: Tell him your people bore a hole at the end of a crack, to give it somewhere to stop.
choices.text_after:
"Where I come from, we bore a hole at the end of a crack," you say. "Just past it. It gives it somewhere to stop."

Finn looks at the crack and then at you. He takes the auger down himself, sets it a thumb's width past the end, and turns it through. Then he leans on the plank. The crack walks into the hole and stays there.

"Somewhere to stop," he says. He tries the words over, to hear how they will sound when he says them to his father. By the time the plank is riveted he has decided that the hole blinds the crack, so that it cannot see where to go next, and he tells you so, as a thing you might like to know.

choices.text: Take the auger off the wall and bore it.
choices.text_after:
You take the auger down from its peg, set it a thumb's width past the end of the crack, and turn it through. Then you lean on the plank. The crack walks into the hole and stays there.

Finn watches all of it and says nothing. He rivets the plank. Some time later a second one starts to go, further along, and he has the auger off the wall before you have moved. He bores it himself, a thumb's width past the end. He does not look at you while he does it, and you can tell from the back of his neck that he would like to.

choices.text: Tell him why a crack runs.
choices.text_after:
"It runs because the end of it is sharp," you say. "All the pull in the plank comes to that one point, and the point tears. Make the end round, and the pull is spread about, and there is nothing to tear."

Finn hears every word. You can see it going in. "Sharp," he says, and feels the end of the crack with his thumbnail.

"Wood has no pull in it," says Orm, from the far end of the shed, without turning round. "It has grain. Bore your hole." Somebody laughs. Finn bores the hole, and the crack walks into it and stops, and nobody in the shed but Finn looks as if that had proved anything.

n_bench.title: Hild's stick
n_bench.text:
The cloths are boiled at a bench against the south wall of the hall, out of the wind. The old woman from last night is feeding a fire under the pot, and a younger one is hanging what comes out of it along a rail.

The old woman is Gyda. She looks at you as a cat looks at a second cat.

The younger one is called Hild, and she has a stick.

::clue hild_stick::

"That edge is the ones we washed with the boiled water," she says. "This edge is the ones we did not, before he came. A cut for every wound, and a cross-cut through it if it went bad." She turns it over for you. One edge has a good many cross-cuts and the other has two. "Gyda says it was the weather. I think weather would be on both edges."

[if occupation == nurse]You sat through three days of lectures on how to do what she has done with a knife and a stick, and you would not have thought of the stick.[else]It takes you a moment. Then you see that she has done, with a knife and a stick, the thing your own people needed several hundred years and a great many dead to think of.[/if]

"Nobody asked you to keep that," Gyda says.

"No," says Hild.
[break]
A woman comes across the yard carrying a child of about three, who is too quiet. He has had a fever for two days, and the flux with it, and this morning he stopped crying, which his mother took for a good sign. His eyes have gone back in his head. Gyda feels his belly and calls for ale with an egg in it.

[if occupation == nurse]You know what you are looking at, and how long he has. It is not the fever. He is running dry. Water with salt and something sweet in it, a spoonful at a time, all day, and most of them live.[else]You know this one, as it happens. It is printed on the back of a packet in every chemist's you have ever stood in. Water, salt and something sweet, a spoonful at a time, all day. It is not the fever that takes them. They run dry.[/if]

choices.text: Tell them it is your grandmother's cure.
choices.text_after:
"My grandmother had a cure for this," you say. "Boiled water, honey, and a pinch of salt. A spoon at a time, for as long as he'll take it."

Gyda has been giving honey for the flux for forty years, and says so. The salt she does not hold with. But a grandmother is an authority she can recognise, having been one for some time, and she lets Hild mix it. The child takes a spoonful, and then another. By noon he has taken half the cup, and his mother has remembered to sit down.

"Whose grandmother?" Hild asks you quietly, cutting the stick. She has started a third edge.

choices.text: Mix it, and start spooning.
choices.text_after:
You take a cup of the boiled water from the bench, stir in honey from Gyda's own crock and a pinch from the salt box, and sit down by the child with the horn spoon you were lent last night. Nobody stops you. It is quite clear that somebody would, if the child had anyone better.

He takes a spoonful, and then another. You go on. By noon he has taken half the cup. Gyda has watched every spoon go in and said nothing, and when the mother asks her what the stranger is giving him she says, "Honey," which is a third of the truth, and the third she can stand behind.

Hild cuts her stick. She has started a third edge.

choices.text: Tell Hild what is happening inside him.
choices.text_after:
You say it to Hild, since she is the one with the stick. "It isn't the fever that kills them. Everything is running out of him, and he's drying up. The water puts it back. The salt makes the water stay, and the honey gets the salt in."

She does not look at you as the hall did last night. She looks at the child, and then at the cup, and you can see her laying the one against the other. "Drying," she says. "Like fish."

"Like fish," Gyda says, a good deal louder, to the mother and to the yard. "He says your boy is drying like a fish." The mother takes the child back onto her own knee. It is Hild who mixes the cup in the end, and Hild who spoons it, and she does it exactly as you said. By noon he has taken half of it. You are standing by the wall.

n_forge.title: The bellows
n_forge.text:
[if hero.sex == female]Aud catches you in the yard and puts a key in your hand, a long iron one with its bit snapped off. "Hrapp can mend that," she says, "and you can wait while he does." It is your first sight of how she gets a person through a door.

[/if]The forge stands apart from everything that can burn. Hrapp is at the anvil when you come in, and he does not stop. He is hoarse this morning. Each time he swallows, he remembers you.

"I am alive," he says at last, to the iron. "I had noticed. You need not have come to see."

There is a boy on the bellows, of about Kol's size and a good deal quieter, and there is something wrong with the bellows. They wheeze. The boy pumps twice for every breath the fire gets.

"Your kinsman mended those," Hrapp says. "They were not broken. He put a tongue of leather inside, so that the air would go one way only, and for a month they blew like the north wind and he told me about it daily. Now the tongue sticks." He turns the iron. "I have kept a count of what he owes this forge."

::clue hrapp_marks::

The first cut, the boy tells you, is the sign that starts your uncle's name. The rest are days.
[break]
[if occupation == welder]You have rebuilt more bellows than you can count. The leather has dried, curled at the edge and caught. It wants taking out, working with fat and putting back with a stitch at the hinge, and it is a quarter of an afternoon's work.[else]You get your head down by the bellows and look. Inside the wooden throat is a flap of leather, hinged at the top. It has dried out and curled, and it is catching on its own edge. You have a cat flap at home that does the same every winter. It wants fat, and a stitch at the hinge.[/if]

choices.text: Tell him your people grease the tongue at every new moon.
choices.text_after:
"At home we grease the tongue at every new moon," you say. "Then it never dries."

"Every new moon," says Hrapp. It is the kind of thing he can do something with. A man can remember a new moon. He sends the boy for the tallow, and you take the tongue out, work the fat into it and stitch it back, and the bellows fetch one long clean breath and the fire goes white.

"He never said anything about the moon," Hrapp says. He sounds almost cheated.

choices.text: Take it out, grease it, and put it back.
choices.text_after:
You pull the peg from the throat of the bellows, draw out the leather, and hold out your hand toward the boy until he works out that what you want is the tallow. You work the fat in, put a stitch at the hinge with Hrapp's own awl, and peg it back. The bellows fetch one long clean breath and the fire goes white.

Hrapp looks at the fire. He looks at you. "He would have talked through the whole of that," he says. It is the nearest thing to thanks that the forge has in it, and the boy stares at him.

choices.text: Tell him why it sticks.
choices.text_after:
"It sticks because the leather has dried," you say. "When it dries it curls, and the curl catches the edge of the hole. The air is pushing it the right way. It just can't get past itself."

Hrapp puts the hammer down, which he has not done since you came in.

"He explained it too," he says. "He explained the bellows, and he explained the fire. And then one night he went down the hall and explained to my brother why his boy was dead." He picks the hammer up again. "Grease it or leave it. Do not tell me about it."

You grease it. The bellows fetch one long clean breath and the fire goes white, and neither of you says a word about that.

n_skald.title: The skald
n_skald.text:
The noon meal is cold, and eaten where people happen to be. [if counter.place >= 3]A girl brings yours to you, which you understand does not happen to everybody.[else]You fetch your own from a board by the door, after the dogs have been spoken to.[/if] Thorgrim asks what kind of use you were. [if road.day == boat]You say you held the end of a plank. Finn, from down the bench, says it was the right end.[elif road.day == bench]You say you fed a child with a spoon. Gyda says, across you, that it was her honey.[else]You say his smith's bellows are blowing. Hrapp, who has come up for his meat, says that this is so, and takes the meat away to eat somewhere else.[/if]

Then the dogs all get up at once, and a man walks in out of the rain as a man walks into his own house.

He is thin, and wet to the thigh, and he has a staff, and a hat he does not take off until he has been looked at in it. The hall is pleased to see him as a hall is pleased to see a pedlar. He has things they want, and they will have to feed him.

"Eyvind," Kol tells you. "He goes between the halls and says who is dead."
[break]
He says, when he has a horn in his hand, that the king's ships are at the mouth of the next fjord but one. He counted eleven. They are taking a tenth of what each farm has, and the names of the men on it. Then he says that he made a verse on the way over the hill, and would the hall like it, and the hall would.

You do not follow all of it. The brass ear does what it can, and gives up where the poetry starts. But you follow enough. It is about a short man from the south with soft hands, who promised a great lord a ship that would outrun the wind, and ate the lord's mutton for a summer, and went into a stone. The hall enjoys it a great deal, Thorgrim least.

Afterwards he comes and sits by you, since you are the newest thing in the room.

"You are the kinsman," he says. "I will want something for the next hall. They will ask me what came after the short man. What came after him?"

choices.text: Tell him the truth: a shed, a door, a letter.
choices.text_after:
You tell him. A shed, two days' ride from any sea. A door with no wall round it. A letter. He listens to the end and does not once stop you, and afterwards he sits for a while, moving his lips.

"A door in a stone," he says. "With no house to it. And a man goes in at one side and does not come out at the other." He is counting on his fingers. "Nobody will believe it. It scans, though." You have the feeling that you have just become a poem, and that it will be told for some time to people who take it for a riddle.

choices.text: Give him something better.
choices.text_after:
You tell him you came by sea, from a country so far south that the ships have two masts, to find a kinsman who had wandered. It is not much of a lie. He improves it while you watch. By the time he has finished his horn there are three ships, and you have left a great house to come, and your kinsman is a kind of holy fool that your people are bound to look after.

"That one will travel," he says. He seems to think he has done you a kindness, and he may have.

choices.text: Tell him to ask again when you have done something.
choices.text_after:
"Ask me again when I've done something," you say.

He looks you over. "That is what the good ones say," he says, "and also the ones who never do anything." He makes a verse anyway, since a skald cannot leave a hall with a hole in his news. In it you are tall, and silent, and came out of the stone at night, and nobody knows what you want. Kol has it by heart before supper.

n_counsel.title: The king's tenth
n_counsel.text:
That evening nobody plays at anything. The fire is built up, the children are sent to the far end, and the hall talks about the king.

There are three things a hall can do, and each has a bench to itself. Bjorn and the older men are for paying. A tenth is a tenth, and they have had worse winters. The young men round Finn, Orm's son, are for the shore and the axes, since eleven ships is not so very many, and Thorgrim lets them say it twice before he asks which of them has ever seen eleven ships. And there is a third thing, said quietly, mostly by the women: that there is land in the west, a summer's sail past the islands, with nobody on it at all. Hild, who helps Gyda with the cloths, says it loudest. Eyvind has met a man who wintered there.

That is what the ship is for. You had thought he wanted to fight in it. He wants to leave in it, with the wind against him and the king behind.
[break]
[if hero.sex == female]It is Aud who asks you, on the cross-bench, low, while the men are shouting. "Your people live a long way off, and have seen more kings than we have. What do they do when one comes?" When you have answered she stands up and says it to the hall as a thing she has heard, and the hall listens to her as it would not have listened to you.[else]"You," Thorgrim says, down the length of the fire. "Unkel's kin. Your people live a long way off, and have seen more kings than we have. What do they do when one comes?"[/if][if occupation == teacher]

It is the one question in this hall that you could answer exactly. You know this king's name, and how long he lasts, and roughly what becomes of the people who sail west. You have taught it on a wet Thursday to children who were not listening. You find you would rather not be the one who knows.[/if]

choices.text: Tell them to count it: the tenth against the ship.
choices.text_after:
"They count it," you say. "What the tenth costs you, every year, for as long as there is a king. What the ship costs you, once. Then they look at the two heaps."

It is not much, and it is the first thing said all evening that a person can do with their hands. Bjorn starts on it with pebbles on the bench. Within a little while there are two heaps, and an argument about whether sheep go in as sheep or as wool, and Thorgrim has stopped looking at the fire and is looking at the heaps.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: kings like this one win.
choices.text_after:
"Kings like this one win," you say. "Where I come from there is always a king in the end. The halls that fought him are in songs. The ones that paid him are still there."

Nobody thanks you for it. The young men look at you as at somebody who has spat on the floor. But Thorgrim nods, slowly, as he might at a bill he had been expecting, and Aud says, to nobody, "And the ones that leave?"

You tell her you do not know what becomes of the ones that leave. [if occupation == teacher]It is the only lie you tell all evening.[else]It is true, and you wish it were not.[/if]

choices.text: Ask who in the hall wants to go.
choices.text_after:
"Before they decide anything," you say, "they ask who wants to go."

Thorgrim looks at you, and then down the hall. "Well?" he says.

Nobody had asked. It takes a long time, and it does not go by benches. Finn wants to go, and his father would sooner be buried here. The woman whose child had the fever wants to go. Gyda says she is too old to be seasick, and will pay the king in advice. Aud does not say, and you notice Thorgrim not asking her.

n_last_night.title: The well
n_last_night.text:
Later, when the fire is low and the hall has gone to its corners, you learn what your uncle did on his last night here.

[if road.first == explain]Aud tells you. She comes and sits where nobody else will, which is beside you, and takes something from the purse at her belt.

"He left the other half," she says. "It was under his bowl. I have not shown it to my brother."

::clue note_half::

"Hrapp has a brother, Ulfar," she says. "One farm up the water. His boy died at harvest. A fever and the flux, and three days. Your kinsman liked the boy, and sat with him. And afterwards, when the ale was in, he went and told Ulfar why." She turns the paper over, though there is nothing on the back. "The well by Ulfar's byre lies below the byre. He said the water had killed the boy. He was very sure, and very sorry, and he said it in front of everyone."

"What did Ulfar hear?"

"That his well was cursed, and that Unkel had known it was, and watched. It was Hrapp who got the knife off him." She gives you the paper. "Ulfar has not sat in this hall since."[elif road.first == hold]It is the boy from the forge who tells you. He has decided, since last night, that anybody who can put Hrapp on the floor is worth knowing, and he tells it in pieces, between looks at the door.

Hrapp has a brother, Ulfar, whose farm is the next one up the water. Ulfar's boy died at harvest, of a fever and the flux, in three days. Unkel had sat with him. And afterwards, in the hall, with the ale in him, Unkel stood up and told Ulfar why. The well by Ulfar's byre lies below the byre, he said. It was the water. He was sorry, the boy says. He was crying. But he kept on saying it.

"Ulfar thought he was being told his well was cursed, and that Unkel had known." The boy shows you, on his own palm, where the knife went. "Hrapp took it off him. So Hrapp has had to be angry with his brother and grateful to his brother's enemy ever since, and he is not made to do both."[else]Nobody tells you. You put it together yourself, as the hall put you together last night, from what is lying about.

There is an empty place on the bench beside Hrapp that nobody sits in. There is a farm one up the water that Kol will not take you to. On the slope behind it, when you walked out before supper, there was a small new mound with white stones laid on it, and below the byre a well with a hurdle across it and a rock on the hurdle.

You ask Kol one question, which is who shut the well. "Ulfar," he says. "After Unkel told him it had killed his boy. He told him in here, in front of everyone. He was crying." Kol thinks about it. "Ulfar cut him. Hrapp is Ulfar's brother, and it was Hrapp who stopped it. That is why Hrapp does the voice. He has to do something."[/if]

He was right about the well. You are as sure of that as he was, and it has done him no more good than it will do you.

choices.text: Sleep, if you can.

n_stone.title: The white stone
n_stone.text:
You go up the hill with Kol before anybody is about. It is a good deal easier going up than it was coming down, and you are getting the measure of the moss.

The smell is still there by the boulder, if you put your face close to the quartz: woodsmoke and low tide, and under them, very faint, the heater in your uncle's shed. Yesterday Kol could smell it from the path. He says that when Unkel first came it was strong enough to bring the dog up from the yard, and that it has come and gone ever since, like the water in the fjord, only slower. He has been keeping an eye on it for a year, he says, in case it turned out to matter.

"It goes somewhere," he says. He is not asking. "He went in there. I saw his back go in, and after that the stone was only a stone." He puts his hand flat on the quartz, where the nine marks are. "Where does it go?"

choices.text: Tell him it goes to a country a very long way off.
choices.text_after:
"A country a long way off," you say. "Further than the ships go."

"Further than the empty land?"

"A good deal further."

He takes that in. You watch him put the stone at the far edge of everything he knows, and then move the edge. "Then the smell is that country," he says. He leans in and takes a long breath of your uncle's heater, and is satisfied. By the time you are back in the yard three people know that the white stone goes to the country past the empty land. None of them is frightened of it, which you had not expected.

choices.text: Tell him the truth.
choices.text_after:
"It goes to this same hill," you say. "A very long time from now. More winters than you could count if you counted all your life. There's no hall. There's a road."

He does not laugh. He looks down at the hall, with the smoke lying along the roof, for long enough that you wish you had said something else.

"Is it still called this?" he says. You tell him you don't know what this is called. He tells you. It is a good name. You promise him you will look, and find that you mean it.

choices.text: Tell him you will tell him when he is older.
choices.text_after:
"I'll tell you when you're older," you say.

He gives you the look that every child of eleven has given every adult who ever said it, in any year you care to name. "Unkel said that," he says. "He said it about the stone, and the beasts in the water, and why the moon follows you home. I am already older than I was when he said it."

He does not ask again. He means to find out by himself, and you do not think it will take him until he is older.

n_surety.title: What you leave
n_surety.text:
Thorgrim is waiting in the yard when you come down, with Aud beside him and most of the hall finding reasons to be within earshot.

"Orm says the weather turns tomorrow," he says. "Kol says the stone is closing. And I say that the last one of you who went up that hill took half a pound of my silver with him." He is not angry. He has the look of a man who has thought about this in the night and got it into an order. "You may go and look for him. I would sooner he were found than not. But you will leave me something, so that I know you mean to come back down."

choices.text: Leave him what you carried.
choices.text_after:
[if kit == bag]You put the bag down in front of him. It is everything you know how to do, with a handle on it. He does not open it. "That is a real thing," he says. "Unkel would not have left his." It goes into the locked end of the hall, behind one of Aud's keys. You feel a good deal lighter, and do not much like it.[elif kit == notebook]You hold out the notebook. Thorgrim takes it, opens it, and studies a page of your uncle's capitals for a while with great attention, upside down. "This is his," he says. "All of what he knew?"

"All of what he wrote down."

He gives it to Aud, who puts it in the purse at her belt. You are fairly sure she will have found somebody to explain the pictures to her before you are over the hill.[else]There is not much left in the sack. You give it to him anyway: the last of the sugar, two cards of needles, the tin. Thorgrim weighs it in his hand. Then, to your surprise, he takes out one card of needles and hands the rest back. "Nobody should go on a journey with nothing to give," he says. "Unkel taught me that, by doing it."[/if]

choices.text: Give him your oath.
choices.text_after:
"I'll swear to it," you say.

They take that more seriously than you had meant it. A ring is fetched from beside the high seat, an iron one as thick as your thumb, and you are shown where to put your hand. Thorgrim says the words and you say them after him, half a beat behind, which is how the brass ear has taught you to do everything. You swear to come back down the hill, with your kinsman or with what he owes.

Nobody smiles. You had thought of it as something to say. You see now that it was something to do, and that you have done it.

choices.text: Ask whoever you worked beside to speak for you.
choices.text_after:
[if road.day == boat]Finn says it before you can ask. "{He} held the right end," he says. "I will stand for {him}." His father looks at him as if he had put a plank on upside down.[elif road.day == bench]It is Hild who steps out, with the stick in her hand. "I will stand for {him}," she says. Gyda makes a noise. "{He} will come back," Hild says, "because I have not finished asking."[else]Nobody is more surprised than Hrapp. "I owe {him} a breath," he says, to the ground. "I will stand for {him}. If {he} does not come back I am quit of it, and if {he} does I am quit of it, and either way I would like it to be over."

It is the least gracious surety anybody in the yard has ever heard, and Thorgrim takes it at once.[/if]

n_goodbye.title: The yard
n_goodbye.text:
You go up at noon, since nobody will let you leave before you have eaten.

[if road.day == boat]Finn walks you to the edge of the stubble. He has a rivet in his hand, one of the clenched iron ones from the fifth plank, and he gives it to you as a thing he has not thought about very hard. "It is the one beside your hole," he says. "It will want replacing anyway. Bring it back, and I will put it in the ship."[elif road.day == bench]Hild walks you to the edge of the stubble. She has cut a second stick, the length of your hand, with nothing on it yet. "One edge for what you see that works," she says. "One for what does not. I want to know whether it is the same there." She does not say where there is. She has plainly decided that it is somewhere.[else]The boy from the bellows walks you to the edge of the stubble, since Hrapp would not be seen to. He gives you a nail. It is a good one, square and newly drawn, and it is the first thing Hrapp has made since the bellows were mended. "He says it is not a gift," the boy says. "He says to say that."[/if]

Aud is standing in the door of the hall with her sleeves pushed back. She does not come down. When she sees you look, she holds up the horn spoon, so that you can see she has it, and goes back in.

choices.text: Go up the hill.

e_door.title: The door
e_door.text:
Kol comes as far as the boulder and no further, and holds the dog.

The smell is almost gone. There is a place on the quartz, under the nine marks, where the rain does not seem to land, and when you put your hand near it the air is warmer and smells of somewhere else. It is not the shed. It is sweeter, like wet cedar and a charcoal fire. Stuck to the rock, under the moss, is a strip of masking tape that you would swear was not there three days ago.

::clue next_label::

You look back once. The hall is where it was, with the smoke lying along the grass of the roof. The keel is a pale line in the door of the boat shed. Kol has let go of the dog to wave with both arms. You have been here three days, and you know a dozen people by name, and one of them is waiting for a ship.

Then you put your hand flat on the warm place, as he must have done nine times, and go where he went.

p_shed.title: The shed
p_shed.text:
Your uncle Walter does not trust telephones, so the news comes by post, on one page, in block capitals pressed hard enough to read from the back.

::clue letter::

He has ended every letter that way since you were nine, including the Christmas cards, which he addresses to her. You are the only person he writes to, and you have never been sure whether to take that as a compliment. He did not say which Saturday. You let that carry you past the first one, and it is the second when you go.

It is two hours of gravel to his place. The yard light is on at noon and his truck is in the yard with the flat you mentioned in April, when he said he was aware of it. The shed door is rolled open a foot for the cat.

Inside, the heater is running for nobody. There is a cup of coffee on the bench with a skin on it, and the radio is on low, where a man is reading out the price of canola.
[break]
Bolted to the slab in the middle of the floor is a door frame, with no door in it and no wall around it. It is seven feet of two-inch square tube, and cables as thick as your wrist run from it to a rack of equipment you cannot name, apart from one item, which is the arc welder that went missing from your mother's garage four years ago. He helped you look for it.

[if occupation == welder]You look at the welds first, because you always do. You gave him a summer of lessons once, and none of it stuck. He has ground every joint flat and painted over it, and nobody does that to a weld they are proud of. Whatever this frame does, those are what is holding it together.[elif occupation == nurse]You look at the bench first, because eleven years have taught you to find the mess before you look at the patient. There is a roll of gauze with its wrapper torn open by teeth, a bottle of the brown antiseptic nobody has stocked since you trained, and a tea towel that will not be used for tea again. Whatever he cut, he dressed it one-handed and in a hurry, and about as well as he does most things.[elif occupation == teacher]You look at the shelf first, because you read people's shelves. There is the Old Norse grammar you lent him two Christmases ago and wrote off, with its spine broken at the verbs. Next to it are a road atlas of Italy and a paperback history of Japan with a bus ticket a third of the way in. He has never been known to finish a book, and you would have said he had never been known to start three.[else]You look at the supply first, because somebody ought to. The cables run back to the panel by the door, where he has pulled the breaker for the grain dryer and fitted something of his own made out of copper bar. There is a scorch on the wall above it in the shape of a hand. Nothing in this building is rated for whatever goes through that frame, and the building has plainly told him so.[/if]

Under a wrench on the bench is half a sheet of paper.

::clue note::

There is a thumbprint beside the W, in something brown. You would like it to be coffee, and coffee does not dry that colour.
[break]
Beside the note is a foam-lined case cut for two of something. One place is empty. In the other is a brass object about the size of a hearing aid, with a hook to sit behind the ear. He has put a strip of masking tape on the lid.

::clue ear_label::

There is a label just like it on the dash of his truck, and you have ridden in the truck.

Through the frame you can see the back wall of the shed, the pegboard and the co-op calendar, all where they belong. The air inside it is a little darker than the air outside it, though, as it is in any doorway, and a draught is coming through that smells of woodsmoke and low tide. The nearest tide is three days' drive from here.

The cat is on a blanket against the far wall, which is as far from the frame as a cat can get without going out in the rain. It has the look of an animal that settled there some days ago.

There is more tape on the frame itself, at eye height.

::clue frame_label::

So you are going, it seems, and the question is what the hand is for. Your work bag is in the truck, since he asked for it. His notebook is on the bench beside the note, a black one gone fat with use, with a rubber band round it. And over the kettle is a shelf he has labelled TRADE, which holds a bag of sugar, a tin of pepper and three cards of steel needles from the fabric shop in town. You had taken that for groceries and a hobby.

choices.text: Fetch your work bag from the truck.
choices.text_after:
The bag is on the passenger seat, under a coat, where it spends its weekends.

You hook the brass thing behind your ear and find it warm, as if it had lately been behind somebody else's. The note goes into your jacket, since a person should have something to show the police. Your phone and your lighter are in your pockets already, where they live.

You step through the frame as you would over a garden hose, without looking down, with your one hand's worth.

place: Nobody has decided what you are.
You have a place by the door, and a use.
You are somebody's guest, and it shows in how you are served.
You have been moved up the bench, into the warm.
You are asked what you think.
Thorgrim would rather you came back than not.
talk: Nobody is talking about you yet.
They are talking about you, kindly enough.
They are explaining you to each other.
People move along the bench when you sit down.
They are saying what they said about your uncle.
Children are called away from you.
There is a verse about you in the next fjord.
It would not take much now.
